config.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists

intro.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function to find the intersection node of two singly linked lists, where the lists may share a common tail. You will learn the core concept of using two pointers to traverse the lists at different speeds to detect the intersection point efficiently. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, linked list node objects, and pointer manipulation. This exercise will help you understand fundamental algorithm design and improve your lesson-solving skills with data structures.
intro.usecase: Finding the intersection of linked lists is crucial in systems that need to identify shared resources or overlapping data streams. For example, in social media platforms, this algorithm can help find mutual friends between two users by comparing their friend lists as linked structures. In version control systems like Git, it's used to find the common ancestor commit when merging two branches. Database systems also apply this pattern when joining tables or finding overlapping query results. Understanding this algorithm helps developers optimize data comparison operations in real applications.

objectives: Construct two linked lists with a common intersection node.
Initialize pointers to traverse each linked list from their heads.
Manipulate pointer movement to handle lists of different lengths.
Apply a two-pointer algorithm to detect the intersection node.
Integrate conditional logic to manage edge cases like no intersection.
Implement a function that returns the intersection node or null.
Control the traversal loop to terminate upon finding the intersection or reaching list ends.

content.body: Have you ever wondered how to find where two separate paths meet? In linked lists, we can't just look at positions like in arrays. Let's learn how to find the intersection point where two linked lists join together.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why we can't use array indexing with linked lists
2. Implement two-pointer traversal to find list intersections
3. Handle edge cases like lists of different lengths
4. Visualize node-by-node movement through both lists
5. Preserve the original head pointers while traversing
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you have two separate chains of connected nodes. List A has nodes: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. List B has nodes: 9 → 8 → 3 → 4 → 5 (they join at node 3). How would you find where they meet? Try to think through it step by step.
content.title: Try it

content.body: You can only look at one node at a time in each list. You can move from a node to its next node, but you can't jump to position 3 directly. How would you move through both lists to find the meeting point?
content.title: Think about movement

content.body: You probably thought about starting at the beginning of each list and moving forward one node at a time. This is the right mindset for linked lists - we can only walk node by node along the chain.
content.title: What you did

content.body: The tricky part is that the lists might be different lengths. If you start at both heads and move one step at a time, you might miss the intersection because you'll be comparing nodes at different positions. Can you think of a way to handle this?
content.title: The challenge

content.body: Remember: with linked lists, we can only move to next (or prev in doubly linked lists); we cannot jump by index. This means we need to be clever about how we traverse. We'll use two pointers that walk through both lists, but we need to account for different starting positions.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Imagine two people walking along different paths that eventually merge. If they walk at the same speed but start at different distances from the merge point, they won't meet at the intersection. They need to adjust their starting positions.

content.body: Here's the clever trick: if we make both pointers travel the same total distance (list A length + list B length), they'll meet at the intersection if one exists. When a pointer reaches the end of one list, it continues from the head of the other list. This way, both pointers travel equal distances to the intersection.
content.title: The approach
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it as two runners on different tracks that eventually merge. If one track is shorter, that runner finishes their track first and then starts running on the other track from the beginning. Both runners cover the same total distance and meet at the merge point.

content.body:
1. Start two pointers at the heads of both lists
2. Move both pointers forward one node at a time
3. When a pointer reaches the end of its list, move it to the head of the other list
4. Continue until both pointers meet (intersection found) or both reach the end (no intersection)
5. The meeting point is either the intersection node or null
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called getIntersectionNode that takes two parameters: headA and headB. Both are heads of linked lists. Return null for now.
steps.hint: Remember the function signature: function getIntersectionNode(headA, headB)
steps.expectedOutcome: A function that takes two linked list heads and returns null
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure your function takes two parameters and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a function called getIntersectionNode with parameters headA and headB.

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create two pointers: pointerA starting at headA and pointerB starting at headB.
steps.hint: Use let to declare variables: let pointerA = headA; let pointerB = headB;
steps.expectedOutcome: Two pointer variables initialized to the head nodes
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure you have both pointerA and pointerB variables.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to create two variables: pointerA and pointerB, starting at headA and headB.

steps.title: Create the traversal loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues as long as pointerA is not equal to pointerB. This is where we'll do our traversal.
steps.expectedOutcome: A while loop that continues while the pointers are not equal
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure your while condition checks if pointerA is not equal to pointerB.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a while loop with the condition: pointerA !== pointerB

steps.title: Move pointerA
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, move pointerA forward. If pointerA is not null, move to its next node. If it is null, reset it to headB.
steps.expectedOutcome: PointerA moves to next node or resets to headB when reaching end
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good. Make sure you handle both cases: when pointerA has a next node and when it's null.

steps.title: Move pointerB
steps.instruction: Now do the same for pointerB. If pointerB is not null, move to its next node. If it is null, reset it to headA.
steps.hint: Add pointerB = pointerB ? pointerB.next : headA; after moving pointerA.
steps.expectedOutcome: PointerB moves to next node or resets to headA when reaching end
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure pointerB resets to headA when it reaches the end.

steps.title: Return the result
steps.instruction: After the while loop ends, return pointerA (which will be equal to pointerB). This will be either the intersection node or null.
steps.hint: Add return pointerA; after the while loop.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function returns either the intersection node or null
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good. Make sure you return pointerA (or pointerB - they're equal).
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: return pointerA; at the end of the function.

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented an elegant solution to find linked list intersections. Remember these key points:

1. Linked lists require node-by-node traversal - we can't jump by index
2. The two-pointer approach with list switching ensures both pointers travel equal distances
3. This handles lists of different lengths automatically
4. The solution is O(n + m) time and O(1) space - very efficient!

This pattern of switching lists is a classic linked list technique that appears in many lessons. Keep practicing walking node by node!
